en: And no life to a demon—
A mountain that could never be broken.
They were the teeming Kyrgyz people’s defense,
A vast black fortress.
While the fierce gray wolf lived,
Though suffering descended upon the world,
We said, ‘Where could calamity be?’
While our warrior sultan lived,
When bored, we hunted deer;
When not, we poor souls
Played ordo for stakes amid loud rejoicing,
Played orompoy amid merry clamor,
Making them say, ‘Ah, the valiant Kyrgyz!’
We raised an uproar against every foe,
Serving as a stronghold that spared no life.
To those who knew and those who saw,
To those who heard and understood,
To any who merely narrowed their eyes at us,
And to the enemy who overran us,
We brought sheer affliction.
We were a broad, mottled mountain range
No living creature could cross.
We were the heroic Kyrgyz people,
Yielding to no one in all the world.
The sultan and stronghold have left the Kyrgyz,
The hero has left the people of the age,
The lion blessed by Khidr has departed.
Our glasslike eyes stare wildly;
Parted from our precious lion,
The nation wails in grief.
Bereft of our dear hero,
With no tail left to swish,
We stand like wild asses.
With no feet to stride forward,
We stand like snakes.
Will we become mounts
That do not even flick their ears as they walk?
When the enemy surrounds us,
Unable to charge and summon courage,
Will we become as the dead?
Will we cease to encamp
At Kan-Jailak, where the people spread?
Heeding no one’s word,
Unable to bear one another,
Will we cease to be a people?
Will this immense, incurable affliction
Leave us in turmoil?
Will painful misery and great conflict
Leave us in a single storm of chaos?
Bereft of our warrior lion,
We have fallen into disaster.
Our eyes dim and wander—
We have become blind.”—
So the nation clamored,
Yellowing like straw,
Amazed at the utter vanity
Of this battered world.
Every living creature
The Creator brought forth and set in motion;
All who knew, saw, or perceived,
The supreme decree of the Creator
Directed toward a single pit.
By His decree He fashioned
The eighteen thousand worlds.
Every living creature
Must cross this ominous black earth.
Oh Ala-Too, whose foothills are gold,
If only the Kyrgyz could dwell there forever!
If only our doomed prince Semetey,
His true kinsman Külchoro,
Poor Bakai and Kanykei,
And the noble lord’s wife Aichürök—
Alas, deceitful world!—
If only these, who should never die,
Had spines of iron!”
The whole nation cried out and wept,
Tormenting their fragile lives,
Unable to endure, lamenting,
Astonished that this exalted, painful world
Was empty at its core,
And marveling at it.
The great lion stood unmoving—
“Father, we have parted forever, dear lion!”—
The doomed hero stood unmoving.
The five valiant heroes united
And began their journey to the land of no return.
They left the settled nation, the teeming people,
Thus abandoned to desolation.
When the warriors departed on their journey,
Who, without wearying his jaw, will whet
The black-bladed battle-axe?
If the vast Kyrgyz nation remains,
Who will lead it without bringing grief?
Who will keep the red-shafted Zulfiqar spear
Sharpened without stirring it?
If the age-old Kyrgyz people remain,
Who will lead them without wavering?
If the precious lion closes his eyes,
There are Chinese on the frontier,
Russians on the right,
A mass of guns before us,
And many hostile foes.
How shall the villages pitch camp?
What remedy will remain
For the few scattered, wandering people?”—
The nation said this with sobs,
And all the heroes grieved.
Everyone old enough to understand
Said, “Now disaster has come,”
And despaired of life.
As the people stood mourning,
The dear lion whose courage was mountainous,
The doomed hero, heavy with grief,
Prepared himself like a hawk.
Into the dear lion’s mouth
Wisdom came from the unseen;
His heart withdrew and turned away,
And his gray-wolf valor showed.
Leaving this wretched world behind,
He bade farewell to the countless people:
“Great and small, old and young,
Elder sisters, sisters-in-law, and younger sisters,
All of you stand here.
White-bearded wise elders,
You too stand here.
My thick-armed tigers,
My stout-limbed heroes,
When the black musket cracks,
You enter battle without tiring.
When the fierce gun snaps,
You enter battle without fear.
Thick-armed and stonehearted,
Stout-limbed heroes;
Warriors who sow wisdom, whose wrath is fierce,
And whose cunning is complete;
My host arrayed before me,
My heroic Kyrgyz bulwark,
My stronghold, you stand here.
My inheritance from my forefathers,
My inexhaustible treasure—
My people, you stand here.
Kara-Kyr, where the people summer,
My stronghold, you stand here.”
The heroes Bakai and Semetey
Spoke softly, leaving solemn words.
From among the five warriors,
The hero Semetey began to speak:
“My dear people, fare you well.
Our journey has wearied and reached its end;
Our hearts have chosen and turned away,
For this wretched world, vain to behold,
Appears ready to lead us onward.
From the mountain I made my landmark,
I clasp your hands in farewell,
Saying, ‘Farewell, remain in peace.’
Our journey has grown old, our eyes shine;
From the fleeting pleasures of the world,
We prepare to ride away, our eyes shining.
Grim death has entered my thoughts;
Those destined to depart are going
To the land of no return.
Our hearts have chosen and turned away;
This vain world, brief as a handspan,
Appears ready to lead us onward.
We have begun to reckon our journey,
O my dear people with your royal seat,
Faithless indeed is this world;
Alas, we are leaving it behind.
Kara-Kyr, where the people summered,
Alas, we are leaving the land behind.
Great people with your sheltering fortress,
Alas, we are leaving the nation behind.
The people and their royal fortress remain,
Children and kin alike remain,
While cruel death has seized my back.
We mounted and set out upon the road,
To the land from which none return.
Now sight will fade and life depart.
O hapless people, your strength will leave you;
The sable cap upon my head—
Who has not worn it with a flourish?
When fortune stood at its height,
All who saw it raised a clamor.
Girding my waist for sacrifice,
Where my cord was cut and my newborn body washed,
My land, like Ala-Too,
From wrathful enemies
I guarded my fortunate Kyrgyz people.
I gave you pacing colts to ride,
Made you laugh and set your hearts at ease,
And gave you fine silk clothes to wear;
Each stream in every valley
I allotted, making each of you rich,
And found many ways to serve you.
O hapless people, for your sake,
Not letting even a breath of wind touch you,
I kept witless enemies
From coming near your lands;
Against every enemy who confronted me,
I turned white deer into cattle,
Driving and claiming them as booty.
O dear people, for your sake,
I turned blue-gray deer into cattle
And claimed every land I sought.
O Kyrgyz, for your sake,
I loaded the cannon,
And destroyed all who opposed me.
Whenever they met me face-to-face,
I drove them all away and destroyed them.
From among the five heroes,
The warrior Semetey began to speak:
“O Kyrgyz of Ala-Too,
I built houses for you,
Planted and tended gardens for you.
All your treasure chests
I filled with wealth of yellow gold.
I fulfilled your every wish,
Made your pastures spacious,
And covered your hillsides with livestock.
Your brave men and nobles—
I made every one of you a khan.
While this bloodthirsty soul still lived,
I made your homeland broad.
To blood-spilling enemies
I never surrendered
Even your barren yearling colt.
I became the khan who ruled the royal camp;
But now, a traveler and stranger,
I am taking leave of this world.
Death has settled upon my heart;
I am departing—farewell—
Along the road from which none return.
The angel has stretched out five fingers;
The decree of the Creator
Has issued its good command.
When the Almighty gives His command,
Does any mortal fail to submit?
If the true God so desires,
Will He not grant a soul
Even seven days of borrowed life?
The fate that has been decreed—
Must not every mortal behold it?
The deep black earth below—
Does it not bury the whole world alike?
Can the earth devour all but leave the soul?
When the black earth swallows the world,
Does not its surface grow rich and fertile?
All else is false; death alone is true.
Cruel death has settled upon my heart;
Now I am returning
To the land from which none return.
We five have set out on the journey.
What my father, lionhearted Manas,
Found severed, he joined;
What was scattered, he gathered;
He rekindled the extinguished fire,
